name: Samarkand — the Registan and Timur's Blue City
scope: The turquoise-domed capital Timur (Tamerlane) built in today's Uzbekistan, the grand crossroads of the Silk Road. T1: three towering madrasas (Islamic colleges) frame the Registan, Samarkand's great plaza whose name means 'sandy place' — the answer is the Registan (teach 'madrasa'). T2: on the Sher-Dor madrasa's portal two great cats chase white does under a rising sun-with-a-face — startling because Islamic art usually avoids living creatures; 'Sher-Dor' means 'lion-bearing' (answer: the forbidden living-creature mosaic). T3: Timur's own tomb, the Gur-e-Amir, is crowned by a ribbed, melon-shaped azure dome that became the model later copied at Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal (answer: the fluted turquoise dome / the dome lineage). T4: Ulugh Beg, Timur's astronomer-grandson, sank a 40-metre stone arc — the Fakhri sextant — into a Samarkand hillside and catalogued over 1,000 stars and the length of the year so precisely his figures stood until Tycho Brahe (answer: the giant buried sextant / observatory). T5: when Soviet scientist Mikhail Gerasimov opened Timur's grave on 20 June 1941, a warning was said to read 'whoever disturbs my tomb unleashes an invader worse than I' — two days later Hitler launched Operation Barbarossa (answer: Gerasimov's 1941 exhumation — flagged as LEGEND/coincidence). Also: the Bibi-Khanym mosque, raised so hugely and hastily from India-campaign loot that it began crumbling within decades; the Shah-i-Zinda 'avenue of tombs' tiled in every shade of blue.
source: Wikipedia (Registan, Gur-e-Amir, Curse of Timur, Ulugh Beg Observatory, Bibi-Khanym Mosque); centralasia-travel.com; St Andrews MacTutor (Ulugh Beg). Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: Scene-led PLACE ladder: Samarkand named in every stem, the answer a concrete Samarkand wonder. Distractors = other real Silk Road marvels (Bukhara's Kalyan minaret, Khiva's Kalta Minor, Isfahan's square) so all four stay live. Invert the wonder — lead with the sun-faced cats, the 40 m arc, the 1941 grave — never 'What is the Registan?'. Teach 'madrasa'/'minaret' before testing. Dinner-test payoff = the Gerasimov-curse rung (flag clearly as LEGEND + coincidence) plus the Timur-dome-to-Taj lineage rung. Timur's conquests are HISTORY — keep every answer the BUILDING/place-fact, not the campaign.
history_overlap: Timur's conquests and the sack that funded Bibi-Khanym are history-bank material — keep answers on the buildings, not the campaigns.

name: Bukhara — the Silk Road 'museum city'
scope: A sacred caravan city in Uzbekistan whose old town survives almost intact. T1: the Kalyan minaret has loomed over Bukhara since 1127 — about 46 m of patterned brick that called the faithful to prayer (answer: the minaret; teach 'minaret'). T2: legend says when Genghis Khan rode in to raze the city he tilted his head back to see the tower's top and his hat fell off; awed, he ordered it spared — the one thing left standing, later nicknamed the 'Tower of Death' for the criminals thrown from it (answer: Genghis spared the tower). T3: the Samanid Mausoleum, a perfect brick cube from the 900s whose woven brick patterns shift with the sun, survived the Mongols only because centuries of flood-silt had BURIED it — the raiders never found it (answer: the tomb saved by being buried in sand — DINNER-TEST payoff). T4: the Ark of Bukhara, a mud-brick citadel raised on the rubble of its own earlier selves, was the fortress-palace of the emirs for over a thousand years (answer: the Ark citadel). T5: Bukhara keeps the whole Silk Road pattern — a domed covered bazaar, caravanserais, and the four-turret Chor Minor gate — earning the name 'museum city' (answer: the intact old town / Chor Minor; teach 'caravanserai').
source: Wikipedia (Kalyan Minaret, Samanid Mausoleum, Ark of Bukhara, Bukhara, Chor Minor); people-travels.com; Atlas Obscura. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, Bukhara named in every stem. Distractors = other real Silk Road towers/tombs (Samarkand's Registan, Khiva's Kalta Minor, the Gur-e-Amir). Invert the wonder — lead with 'the hat that fell' and 'the tomb saved by sand,' never 'What is the oldest mausoleum?'. Accuracy rail: the Genghis-hat detail is LEGEND (flag it), but the sparing of the minaret and the silt-burial of the Samanid tomb are real. Teach 'minaret'/'caravanserai' before testing.

name: Khiva — the walled desert city
scope: A fortified oasis town in Uzbekistan, the last caravan stop before the Karakum desert crossing to Persia. T1: Khiva's inner town, the Itchan Kala, is wrapped in mud-brick walls about 10 m high — a whole walled city you can still walk inside (answer: the walled inner town). T2: the fat, stubby Kalta Minor minaret glows solid turquoise from base to top — it is UNFINISHED: its khan died in 1855 and it froze at about 29 m instead of becoming Central Asia's tallest tower (answer: the unfinished minaret — invert with 'why is the gorgeous tower so SHORT?'). T3: inside the Djuma (Friday) Mosque a forest of more than 200 carved wooden columns holds up a flat roof, some pillars over a thousand years old (answer: the wooden-column forest). T4: Itchan Kala was the FIRST place in all Central Asia named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, in 1991 (answer: first Central-Asian World Heritage site). T5: Khiva's skyline of minarets, madrasas and palaces is so perfectly preserved that the whole town looks frozen in time (answer: the 'time-frozen' old town).
source: Wikipedia (Khiva, Itchan Kala); UNESCO WHC #543; Advantour. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, Khiva/Itchan Kala named in every stem. Distractors = other real walled/desert Silk Road towns (Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv). Invert — the Kalta Minor rung leads with its beauty and asks why it is so SHORT (answer: the khan died, it was never finished). Dinner-test payoff = the unfinished squat turquoise minaret. Khiva's slave-market past is at most a light factual mention — keep every answer on the PLACE/architecture.

name: Lahore — the Mughal city of mosque and garden
scope: The Mughal heart of the Punjab, in present-day Pakistan. T1: the Badshahi Mosque, built by emperor Aurangzeb in 1673, is a vast red-sandstone mosque whose courtyard holds tens of thousands of worshippers — for three centuries the largest mosque on Earth (answer: the Badshahi Mosque). T2: across from it the Lahore Fort hides the Sheesh Mahal, a 'palace of mirrors' whose walls and ceiling are set with thousands of tiny mirror-tiles that turn a single candle into a galaxy (answer: the mirror palace). T3: Shah Jahan's Shalimar Gardens step down the land in three terraces threaded with hundreds of fountains — a Persian charbagh, a four-part 'paradise garden' fed by a canal dug for miles (answer: the terraced fountain garden; teach 'charbagh'). T4: the fort's outer 'Picture Wall' is a giant mosaic of glazed tile showing elephants, camels and polo games — one of the largest tiled murals in the world (answer: the Picture Wall). T5: the nearby Wazir Khan Mosque (1634) is so densely covered in fresco and 'kashi' tilework it is called 'a jewel on the palm of Lahore' (answer: the tiled Wazir Khan mosque).
source: Wikipedia (Badshahi Mosque, Lahore Fort, Shalimar Gardens Lahore, Wazir Khan Mosque); UNESCO WHC #171; Britannica. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, Lahore in every stem, each answer a concrete Lahore monument. Distractors = other real Mughal works (Delhi's Jama Masjid/Red Fort, Agra Fort, Kashmir's Shalimar). Invert — lead with 'one candle becomes a galaxy' for the Sheesh Mahal. Teach 'charbagh'/'minaret' before testing. Dinner-test payoff = the mirror palace. LANE BORDER: Lahori food is COOKING-bank — do NOT seed a dish rung; keep answers on mosque/garden/fort.

name: Delhi — the city of seven cities
scope: India's layered capital, rebuilt on the Yamuna plain again and again. T1: the Qutb Minar, begun in 1199, spirals 72.5 m into the sky in red sandstone and marble — the tallest brick minaret in the world (answer: the Qutb Minar). T2: beside it stands a 7-metre iron pillar forged about 1,600 years ago in the Gupta age that has barely rusted — its iron holds just enough phosphorus to grow a thin, self-healing protective skin (answer: the rust-free iron pillar; the phosphorus/misawite film is the mechanism — DINNER-TEST payoff). T3: the Quwwat-ul-Islam beside the Minar was India's first mosque — and its carved columns were reused from 27 demolished Hindu and Jain temples, still plainly visible in the stone (answer: the first mosque, built from temple stones — state honestly). T4: Humayun's Tomb (1560s) was India's first great garden-tomb, a red-sandstone mausoleum set in a four-part charbagh, its double dome linking Samarkand's Gur-e-Amir to the Taj Mahal (answer: the first garden-tomb / the dome lineage; teach 'charbagh'). T5: Shah Jahan's Red Fort (Lal Qila, 1648) once held the jewelled Peacock Throne, and its marble Hall of Private Audience is inscribed 'If there is a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this' — a canal called the 'Stream of Paradise' once flowed through its palaces (answer: the Red Fort / the paradise couplet). Frame: Delhi is nicknamed the city of 'seven cities' for its stacked ruined capitals.
source: Wikipedia (Qutb Minar, Iron pillar of Delhi, Qutb complex, Humayun's Tomb, Red Fort); Britannica; UNESCO WHC #232/#233. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time (esp. Red Fort couplet + Peacock Throne).
framing_note: PLACE ladder, a Delhi monument named in every stem. Distractors = other real Indian monuments (Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri's Buland Darwaza, Lahore's Badshahi Mosque). Invert — lead with 'a 1,600-year iron pillar that won't rust' → answer the phosphorus self-healing film (put the mechanism in the ANSWER, never the stem). Dinner-test payoff = the rust-free iron pillar. HONEST-BOTH-WAYS rail: the first-mosque-from-temple-stones rung states the spoliation plainly, no polemic and no smug framing. Keep the Peacock-Throne rung on the throne-as-place-treasure.
history_overlap: Nader Shah's 1739 sack (the Peacock-Throne looting) and the 1947 Independence-Day flag-raising are history-bank episodes — keep the Red Fort answers on the place and its treasures, not the invasion or independence narrative.

name: The Taj Mahal (Agra)
scope: The white marble tomb on the Yamuna at Agra, built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. T1: the Taj is a tomb built in grief — Mumtaz died in 1631 bearing their child, and the mourning emperor raised it over her (answer: it is a wife's tomb, born of grief — not a palace). T2: its white Makrana marble seems to change colour through the day — pink-tinged at dawn, dazzling white at noon, gold under the moon — because the translucent stone drinks the light (answer: the colour-shifting marble). T3: every flower on its walls is inlaid STONE, not paint — pietra dura, thousands of cut chips of jade, carnelian and lapis set flush into the marble (answer: the pietra dura inlay; teach the term). T4: the four minarets ringing the platform lean slightly OUTWARD on purpose, about 2.7 degrees, so that in an earthquake they would topple away from the dome instead of onto it (answer: the deliberately tilted minarets — the engineering; DINNER-TEST payoff). T5: the whole complex is almost perfectly mirror-symmetrical — the ONE thing that breaks the symmetry is Shah Jahan's own cenotaph, set off-centre beside Mumtaz's after he died a prisoner (answer: the emperor's off-centre tomb breaks the symmetry). Also: from Agra Fort's Musamman Burj the deposed Shah Jahan spent his last years gazing across the river at the Taj; the fabled matching 'Black Taj' is LEGEND/unproven.
source: Wikipedia (Taj Mahal); Britannica; History.com. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, the Taj named in every stem, each answer a concrete Taj fact. Distractors = other real marble/Mughal tombs (Humayun's Tomb, Gur-e-Amir, Bibi-ka-Maqbara, Itmad-ud-Daula the 'Baby Taj'). Invert — lead with 'why do the four towers lean outward?' → the earthquake-safety answer. Dinner-test payoff = the tilted minarets. ACCURACY rails: label the 'Black Taj' as LEGEND, and DEBUNK the 'workers' hands cut off' myth if a distractor tempts it; the marble is Makrana. The dome descends from Samarkand's Gur-e-Amir via Humayun's Tomb — a cross-place lineage note, not a separate fact.
history_overlap: Shah Jahan's deposition by his son Aurangzeb is a history-bank episode — the Agra-Fort rung stays on the place/the VIEW, not the war of succession.

name: Fatehpur Sikri — the abandoned red city
scope: The perfect Mughal capital Akbar built and then walked away from, near Agra. T1: Fatehpur Sikri is a whole imperial city of red sandstone — palaces, courts and a great mosque — that Akbar raised in the 1570s and abandoned within about 15 years (answer: the abandoned 'ghost' capital). T2: it was left empty mainly because it ran out of WATER — the rocky ridge simply could not keep the growing city supplied (answer: water shortage — invert with 'why abandon a brand-new capital?'). T3: its gateway, the Buland Darwaza, soars about 54 m — often called the 'highest gateway in the world' — built to mark Akbar's Gujarat victory (answer: the giant victory-gate). T4: the Panch Mahal is a five-storey open pavilion of columns that shrinks tier by tier like a wedding cake — a 'wind-catcher' raised to trap the breeze in the summer heat (answer: the five-tier wind palace). T5: Akbar built here to honour the Sufi saint Salim Chishti, who had foretold he would finally get a son — the saint's delicate white marble tomb still sits inside the mosque courtyard (answer: the saint's tomb / why he built here).
source: Wikipedia (Fatehpur Sikri, Buland Darwaza, Panch Mahal); UNESCO WHC #255; Grokipedia (Panch Mahal page). Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, Fatehpur Sikri named in every stem. Distractors = other real deserted/Mughal sites (Mandu, Hampi, Delhi's Tughlaqabad, Agra Fort). Invert — lead with 'a flawless new capital emptied in 15 years — why?' → the water answer. Dinner-test payoff = abandoned-for-water. Teach 'Sufi' lightly. Akbar's court religious debates here are HISTORY — keep answers on the BUILDINGS and the water/place-fact.

name: Jaipur — the Pink City and its stone sky-machines
scope: A planned royal city in Rajasthan, laid out on a grid in 1727 by the astronomer-king Sawai Jai Singh II. T1: Jaipur's whole old town is washed a single terracotta pink, earning it the name the 'Pink City' (answer: the Pink City). T2: it was painted pink in 1876 to welcome one royal guest — the visiting Prince of Wales, later Edward VII — because pink was the colour of hospitality (answer: painted for a royal visit — invert with 'why is a whole city one colour?'). T3: at the Jantar Mantar, Jai Singh built astronomy instruments as BUILDINGS you climb — the Samrat Yantra is a stone sundial about 27 m tall that tells the time to roughly two seconds (answer: the giant climbable stone sundial). T4: the Hawa Mahal, the 'Palace of Winds,' is a five-storey honeycomb facade pierced by 953 tiny latticed windows so royal women could watch the street unseen while breezes cooled the rooms (answer: the 953-window palace). T5: above the city, Amber (Amer) Fort mirrors itself in Maota Lake, and its own Sheesh Mahal blazes with mirror-work that lights the whole hall from a single flame (answer: Amber Fort / its mirror hall). Frame: the grid plan by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya made Jaipur one of India's first fully planned cities.
source: Wikipedia (Jaipur, Jantar Mantar Jaipur, Hawa Mahal, Amer Fort); Rajasthan Tourism; BBC Sky at Night. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, Jaipur or its monument named in every stem. Distractors = other real Rajasthan/Indian sites (Udaipur's lake palace, Jodhpur the 'Blue City,' Jaisalmer the 'Golden City,' Delhi's Jantar Mantar). Invert — lead with 'a 27 m sundial accurate to 2 seconds' → answer 'a sundial.' Dinner-test payoff = the climbable giant sundial and the 953 windows. Settled wonder — vision not engaged; no food/animal drift.

name: Varanasi — the eternal city on the Ganges
scope: One of the oldest continuously lived-in cities on Earth, holy to Hindus, on the curving north bank of the Ganges (also called Kashi or Benares). T1: Varanasi's riverfront is a long staircase of stone 'ghats' — broad steps leading straight down into the Ganges where the whole city bathes, prays and gathers at dawn (answer: the ghats; teach 'ghat'). T2: it is among the oldest CITIES still lived in — its lanes have stayed alive for well over 3,000 years, so it is called a 'living' ancient city (answer: one of the world's oldest living cities). T3: at the Manikarnika ghat, funeral pyres burn day and night beside the river, and Hindus believe a soul cremated here escapes the cycle of rebirth (moksha) — a sacred fire kept alight for centuries (answer: the never-quenched cremation fire — DINNER-TEST payoff, treated with dignity). T4: each dusk at the Dashashwamedh ghat priests swing tiered brass lamps in the Ganga Aarti, a fire-and-chant ceremony offered to the river itself (answer: the river fire-ceremony). T5: Hindus call the city Kashi, 'the City of Light,' and hold it to be the city of the god Shiva — one of the holiest places in all Hinduism to die (answer: Shiva's city / the holiest place to die).
source: Wikipedia (Varanasi, Manikarnika Ghat, Dashashwamedh Ghat); Britannica; Atlas Obscura. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, Varanasi or its ghat named in every stem. Distractors = other real sacred rivers/cities (Haridwar, Prayagraj's Sangam, the Nile, the Jordan). Teach 'ghat.' Invert — lead with 'a fire that has never gone out' → the eternal cremation ground. Dinner-test payoff = the cremation-fire moksha rung. VISION RAIL: this is a sacred death-ritual — describe it on Hindus' own terms with dignity, NO smug secular dismissal and NO morbid sensationalism; frame it plainly as a place of hope for liberation.

name: The Kathmandu Valley — city of a thousand temples
scope: A high Himalayan valley in Nepal packed with three ancient royal cities and their temple-squares. T1: at the hearts of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur stand three Durbar ('palace') Squares — open plazas crowded with tiered wooden pagoda-temples around the old kings' palaces (answer: the Durbar squares). T2: on a hill above the valley rises the white dome of Swayambhunath, where a pair of huge painted 'Buddha eyes' gaze out from all four sides of the spire, watching every direction at once (answer: the all-seeing Buddha eyes; teach 'stupa'). T3: wild monkeys overrun Swayambhunath's long stairway, giving it the nickname the 'Monkey Temple' (answer: the Monkey Temple — the PLACE/name). T4: across the valley, Boudhanath is one of the largest stupas in the world — a vast white mound ringed by pilgrims walking clockwise round it spinning prayer wheels (answer: the giant stupa Boudhanath). T5: the valley's tiered pagoda roof-style was carried to China by the Nepali architect Arniko in the 1200s — the East-Asian 'pagoda' owes a debt to Kathmandu (answer: the pagoda exported to China — DINNER-TEST payoff). Note: a 2015 earthquake toppled several Durbar-square temples, since rebuilt.
source: Wikipedia (Kathmandu Valley, Swayambhunath, Boudhanath, Araniko); UNESCO WHC #121. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, a Kathmandu-Valley site named in every stem. Distractors = other real stupas/temple-cities (Lhasa's Jokhang, Bagan, Borobudur, Sanchi). Teach 'stupa.' Invert — lead with 'eyes that watch all four directions' → Swayambhunath. Dinner-test payoff = the Buddha eyes and the pagoda-exported-to-China rung. LANE BORDER: the monkeys are an ANIMAL aside — keep that answer the PLACE-name ('Monkey Temple'), never monkey behaviour/biology. VISION: sacred Buddhist/Hindu sites, handled respectfully on their own terms.

name: Lhasa — the Potala Palace above the roof of the world
scope: The sacred capital of Tibet, set on a plateau about 3,650 m up in the Himalaya. T1: the Potala Palace climbs 13 storeys up the Red Hill above Lhasa, a white-and-crimson fortress of more than 1,000 rooms — for centuries the winter home of the Dalai Lamas (answer: the Potala Palace). T2: it stands at roughly 3,700 m on Marpo Ri ('Red Hill'), its top some 300 m above the valley floor — one of the HIGHEST palaces on Earth (answer: the world's highest palace / its dizzying altitude — invert with the number as hook). T3: the 5th Dalai Lama began the present palace in 1645; the outer shell took just three years but the painted, gilded interior took 45 more (answer: the 5th Dalai Lama's palace). T4: at the city's heart the Jokhang Temple is the holiest shrine in all of Tibetan Buddhism — pilgrims prostrate full-length again and again toward its doors (answer: the Jokhang, the holiest temple). T5: around the Jokhang runs the Barkhor, a pilgrim circuit walked always CLOCKWISE by a slow river of pilgrims turning prayer wheels (answer: the Barkhor pilgrim circuit).
source: Wikipedia (Potala Palace, Jokhang, Barkhor, Lhasa); Britannica; New World Encyclopedia. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, Lhasa/the Potala named in every stem. Distractors = other real high/holy places (Bhutan's Tiger's Nest, Ladakh's Thiksey, Nepal's Boudhanath, Machu Picchu). Invert — lead with '3,700 m up, 13 storeys, 1,000 rooms' → the Potala. Dinner-test payoff = the world's-highest-palace altitude rung. VISION RAIL: respect the sacred site on its own terms; state Tibet as timeless geographic fact (a high-plateau Himalayan capital) and DO NOT editorialize on the China–Tibet political dispute.
history_overlap: Tibet's 1950 annexation and the Dalai Lama's 1959 exile are history/current-events — keep every answer on the buildings and the plateau, not the political dispute.

name: Mohenjo-daro — the 4,500-year-old grid city
scope: A ruined city of the Indus Valley Civilisation on the plain of Sindh, in present-day Pakistan, built around 2500 BCE. T1: Mohenjo-daro's streets run in a straight GRID crossing at right angles — a city planned on a drawing board 4,500 years ago, long before Athens or Rome (answer: the planned grid city — a full civilisation, not 'primitive'). T2: under those streets ran covered brick DRAINS carrying waste out of town, and ordinary houses had their own wells and bathrooms — the world's earliest citywide plumbing (answer: the ancient covered sewer/drainage system — DINNER-TEST payoff). T3: at its centre sits the Great Bath, a watertight brick tank sealed with tar and kept fresh by drains — the oldest known public water tank in the world (answer: the Great Bath). T4: the people left thousands of stamp-seals carved with animals and a script of tiny signs that NO ONE has ever deciphered — we still cannot read their language (answer: the undeciphered Indus script). T5: after a thousand years the city was simply abandoned — perhaps the Indus river shifted its course — and even its real name was forgotten; 'Mohenjo-daro' just means 'Mound of the Dead' (answer: the mysteriously abandoned, re-found city).
source: Wikipedia (Mohenjo-daro, Great Bath, Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation, Indus script); National Geographic. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, Mohenjo-daro named in every stem. Distractors = other real ancient cities (Ur, Harappa, Catalhoyuk, Babylon). Invert — lead with 'covered drains under every street 4,500 years ago' → the sewer system. Dinner-test payoff = citywide plumbing older than Rome. VISION RAIL: present the Indus people as a sophisticated FULL civilisation — world-leading urban engineering — never 'mysterious primitives'; the undeciphered script is a genuine open puzzle, stated as such, not mysticised. Seals show animals but the ANSWER is the SCRIPT/place-fact, not animal biology.

name: Amritsar — the Golden Temple in its sacred pool
scope: The holiest shrine of the Sikhs, in the Punjab city of Amritsar, India. T1: the Harmandir Sahib sits on a marble island in the middle of a great square pool, a golden shrine you reach by a single causeway across the water (answer: the temple in the pool). T2: its upper storeys and dome are sheathed in real gold — about 400 kg of gold leaf that blazes in the pool's reflection at sunrise (answer: the gold covering — invert with 'why does the water seem to catch fire at dawn?'). T3: the pool itself is the Amrit Sarovar, the 'pool of nectar' that gives the city its very name; pilgrims bathe in water believed to heal (answer: the sacred nectar-pool). T4: the temple has a door on EACH of its four sides — deliberately open to people of every direction and every caste — and its entrance sits BELOW street level, so everyone must step DOWN, in humility, to enter (answer: the four open doors / step-down humility — DINNER-TEST payoff). T5: its free community kitchen, the langar, seats anyone — rich, poor, any faith — on the floor as equals and serves around 100,000 free meals every single day (answer: the world's largest free kitchen).
source: Wikipedia (Golden Temple, Amrit Sarovar); Britannica; Incredible India. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
framing_note: PLACE ladder, the Golden Temple/Amritsar named in every stem. Distractors = other real gilded/sacred sites (Kyoto's Kinkaku-ji, Bangkok's Wat Phra Kaew, the Shwedagon, Varanasi's temples). Invert — lead with the pool 'catching fire' at dawn → the gold. Dinner-test payoff = the four open doors / the langar feeding 100,000 a day. LANE BORDER: the langar is a CULTURAL-CREATION/equality fact of the PLACE — keep the answer the KITCHEN-and-equality wonder, not a dish (dishes are COOKING-bank). VISION: sacred Sikh site on its own terms.
history_overlap: The 1984 Operation Blue Star is charged modern history — out of lane; keep every answer on the shrine, the pool, the doors and the langar.
